title: Excuses (Luke 14:15–24)
hook: a field, oxen, a marriage: good reasons to miss the feast

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lowest seat, Proverbs's advice, and a host who says friend, go up higher. Did you let someone else go first? Day five hundred fifty-five.

Sorry, can't make it tonight, something's come up. Most of us have sent that message. Some of us have sent it this week. Usually the reason is real enough: work ran late, the kids are tired, we just need a night in. Back at the same dinner table, a guest says something pious and safe: "Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God." A lovely thought about a feast someday. Jesus answers with a story about a feast right now, and about the very human art of the polite excuse.

A man prepares a great supper and invites many. In that world, guests were often invited ahead of time, then a servant came to fetch them when the meal was ready. That's this moment. The servant goes out with the message, in the King James Bible: "Come; for all things are now ready." The lamb is roasted. The bread is baked. And then: "they all with one consent began to make excuse." All of them. Listen to the excuses, because they're good ones. "I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused." The second: "I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to prove them." Ten oxen, a big purchase; he wants to test them. The third doesn't even ask to be excused: "I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come." Land, business, family. Not one of them is a bad thing. Some commentators point out that nobody buys a field without seeing it first, or oxen without trying them, so the excuses may be thinner than they sound. Either way, the effect is the same. The host is left with a feast and an empty hall. He's angry, and then he does something astonishing. Go out quickly, he tells the servant, into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind. And when there's still room, go further, out to the highways and hedges. The feast happens anyway. The table fills. The story isn't against fields, oxen or marriages. It's about what happens when good things become the reason we miss the best thing. And in the story the invitation never closes: the servant keeps going out until the house is full.
screen: then, large: `THEY ALL WITH ONE CONSENT BEGAN TO MAKE EXCUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say yes to one invitation. Settle and breathe. Think back over the last few weeks. What did you say no to? A call from an old friend, a community event, a quiet time of prayer you kept postponing, a walk someone suggested. Which of those noes were honest rest, and which were a field and five oxen? Don't judge yourself. Just notice. Then choose one invitation, already waiting or soon to come, and decide now to say yes. If you pray, you can listen for the words: come, for all is ready. The bell holds the time.
Excuses. A field, five yoke of oxen and a new marriage: good reasons, given all at once, to miss a feast that was already ready.
Your line: come, for all is ready. Today, when an invitation comes, notice whether your no is honest rest or a field and five oxen, and if it's the oxen, say yes. Day five hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Many Christians hear this story as an invitation to worship and to the Lord's Supper, and some churches echo the servant's words when they invite people to the table at communion.

fork.reveal: he sends into the streets and lanes, then the highways and hedges, "that my house may be filled."

original.note: Greek: to beg off, to make excuse. what all the guests did, with one consent.

trapdoor: what you thought: rude guests who didn't want to come.
what it means: good things, land, work, family, become the reasons people miss the best thing, and the feast fills anyway.
what a scholar hears: guests were invited ahead and fetched when the meal was ready, so refusing at the last call was a public insult.

notes: Year one (day 34, 'there's room at the table') covered this parable from the host's side; this day focuses on the excuses.
Double invitation custom and the 'thin excuses' reading (field unseen, oxen untested) follow commentators such as Kenneth Bailey; presented as 'some commentators'. Confirm.
The carry 'come, for all is ready' is the index line, a compression of KJV 14:17 'Come; for all things are now ready.'
'Compel them to come in' (14:23) was later used to justify coercion; the script paraphrases 14:23 without that phrase. A Keeper may want to address it elsewhere.

Audit (second sample): the teach no longer ends on 'the invitation still stands' (it read as an appeal to the listener); the carry now keeps the practice's line between honest rest and an excuse instead of 'say yes' to everything.
